stories.headline: More Than $405 Million in Ads Flood Top Midterm Races in Final Week
stories.summary:
More than $405 million will be spent on advertising in the final week of the midterm elections across the top 15 House and Senate races, according to AdImpact data as of Wednesday. The figure is expected to keep climbing before Election Day on Tuesday, and it shows where each party sees the best chance to make a late impression on voters.

Republicans are on track to outspend Democrats in Senate races, with at least $143 million in ads from Oct. 27 through Nov. 3. Their largest reservations are $25.5 million for Mike Rogers in Michigan's open seat, $24 million for Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio and $20 million to boost Ken Paxton in Texas. Democrats have reserved more than $119 million for the top 15 races, including $20.3 million for Sherrod Brown in Ohio, $18.5 million in Kansas against Sen. Roger Marshall and $16.4 million in Iowa. The Ohio race has drawn upwards of $500 million in total spending from both parties.

The allocations suggest differing strategic views. Democrats are spending little in Minnesota, where Republicans see a tightening race, and in Florida. Both parties are putting more than $16 million combined into South Carolina, where interim Sen. Darline Graham faces Democrat Annie Andrews. Democrats are spending modestly in North Carolina and Georgia, where their candidates, Roy Cooper and Jon Ossoff, have held sizable polling leads. Republicans are also on pace to outspend Democrats in House races, with nearly $73 million for their top contests.

stories.headline: Update: Leak of Data on More Than 41,000 DHS Personnel Is Third Government Disclosure in a Month
stories.summary:
Details of more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors were published online Wednesday in what appears to be an unprecedented breach. The records include names, work addresses and phone numbers for staff at Customs and Border Protection, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. More than 21,000 of those listed work for CBP and nearly 6,600 for ICE.

The data also named dozens of previously unknown operations, the agents who led them, and technology used in the work, including tools from Cellebrite and Palantir. A group calling itself the Department of Peace said it obtained the profiles through Okta, a single sign-on service, and the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and researcher maia crimew published them in a database called Icepick. The hackers cited Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin's July pledge to turn up the heat on ICE.

A DHS spokesperson said the agency is aware of a potential breach and is working to address it, adding that it takes threats against its employees seriously. DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best said the aim was to replace anonymity with accountability and that the release was not meant as a directory of every agent. Critics, including commentators writing about national security, have warned the exposure of personnel creates safety and counterintelligence risks, while transparency advocates argue it reveals oversight of covert operations and deportation programs. It is the third government data disclosure in recent weeks.

stories.headline: Ethiopia Acquires 12 Russian Su-35 Jets as Tigray Fighting Intensifies
stories.summary:
Ethiopia has received 12 Su-35 fighter jets from Russia, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said while attending the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow. He called the acquisition a milestone for Ethiopia's defense capacity and said the country plans to buy four S-400 air defense systems. Abiy said the deals were agreed several years ago and the aircraft arrived ahead of schedule.

Abiy described Vladimir Putin as a close friend and said Ethiopia is now the first sub-Saharan African country to own such advanced combat technology. He argued that without such capability, surviving as a country in the region would become difficult. A military analyst told BBC Amharic the purchases suggest preparation for possible wars with other countries, not just internal conflicts, and could help protect assets such as the Renaissance Dam.

The announcement follows fighting that began last month in northern Tigray between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front, with each side accusing the other of violating the 2022 deal that ended the earlier civil war. Ethiopia accuses neighboring Eritrea of backing the TPLF. Ethiopia has relied heavily on drones from Turkey and China in recent conflicts, and Abiy said drones remain important alongside fourth-generation jets.

stories.headline: Conservative Activist James O'Keefe Charged With Unlawful Voting and Identity Theft in Minnesota
stories.summary:
Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty charged conservative provocateur James O'Keefe and influencer Cam Higby on Wednesday with felony unlawful voting and identity theft. Prosecutors say the two entered polling places during Minnesota's Aug. 11 primary and identified themselves using the names of registered voters without those voters' knowledge or permission. Moriarty said they also used the names of deceased voters and that investigators do not know where the names came from.

The pair recorded the encounters with hidden cameras while disguised and posted the videos online. O'Keefe said they wore Muslim garb, including a niqab, to expose what he called the lunacy of Minnesota's vouching system, which lets a registered voter vouch for up to eight others. Moriarty said they stopped short of signing the voter oath but that state law bars misrepresenting identity when applying for a ballot. They will receive court summonses rather than be jailed.

Secretary of State Steve Simon, whose office alerted prosecutors, said the men revealed their ignorance of how the laws work and that Minnesota has zero tolerance for lawbreaking at polling places. Neither man immediately commented. The case comes as President Trump and allies press claims of voter fraud and the administration targets Democratic-run states over voter rolls, while Democrats and election officials say such stunts undermine confidence and break the law.

stories.headline: Update: Democrats Lead Generic Ballot by 8 Points as Midterms Near; Judge Rejects DOJ Bid on California Mail Ballots
stories.summary:
With five days until the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the New York Times and Nate Silver polling average shows Democrats leading the generic congressional ballot by 8.2 points as of Oct. 26. President Trump's average approval rating stands at 37 percent in Silver's tracker. Nearly 40 million votes have already been cast, and all 435 House seats and one-third of the Senate are on the ballot.

On Wednesday, U.S. District Judge David Carter, a Clinton appointee, declined to order California officials to segregate and not count mail ballots tied to roughly 20,000 people the Justice Department claims are noncitizens. Carter warned the request would "wreak havoc" on elections already underway. Critics called the request legally thin and designed to cast doubt on results, while supporters of the administration framed it as an effort to safeguard election integrity. The Justice Department is also deploying a record 1,000 election monitors nationwide, including to Maine.

In Alaska, the New York Times reported that operatives aligned with Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign helped recruit a candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan to appear on the ballot against Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. Peltola's campaign and national Democrats deny involvement. Trump called it "voter fraud at the highest level" and said Peltola should be barred from the race, while Sen. Lisa Murkowski demanded the "truth." Democratic strategists have compared it to past GOP-aligned efforts to boost third-party candidates.

Trump campaigned in Ohio for Sen. Jon Husted, who is in a tight race with Sherrod Brown, while former President Obama rallied in Georgia, saying of Republicans, "These are not serious people." Democrats need to flip four GOP-held Senate seats for a majority, and control may hinge on about a dozen races.

stories.headline: Update: Netanyahu Bloc Leads Israeli Vote Count but Neither Side Reaches Majority
stories.summary:
With roughly 85 to 90 percent of ballots counted, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and its allies were on track for about 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. That is well short of the 61 needed to govern. The opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot also fell short, even though exit polls had suggested it might lead.

Turnout was the highest in nearly three decades. Arab parties are projected to win 18 to 19 seats, an unprecedented showing, and the two main blocs appear unable to form a government without relying on them. Netanyahu's bloc lost seats but emerged as the largest grouping.

BBC analysts said the most likely outcome is an impasse, potentially leading to new elections. Weeks of coalition negotiations are expected, with ultra-Orthodox draft disputes and Arab party participation among the key obstacles. The result comes amid regional tension, including concerns about a possible renewed war with Iran.

stories.headline: Update: FDA Scientists Opposed HHS Plan to Ease Access to Unproven Peptide Drugs, AP Reports
stories.summary:
Most Food and Drug Administration scientific staff opposed a plan to ease access to unproven peptide drugs favored by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., according to six people familiar with its development who spoke to the Associated Press anonymously. The policy document, posted Wednesday by HHS, was driven almost entirely by the department, and FDA staff had limited input.

The policy directs the FDA not to take enforcement action against specialty compounding pharmacies that sell about six wellness peptides, including BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV. Under existing rules these substances would be illegal drugs because they have not undergone FDA review for safety and effectiveness. They are promoted in the wellness industry for building muscle, healing injuries and boosting energy.

HHS originally wanted a formal regulation adding the peptides to a list of substances deemed safe for compounding. FDA officials said staff had major safety concerns and would not support that, so HHS shifted to an enforcement-discretion approach. Kennedy has called himself a "big fan" of peptides and has described using BPC-157 for a muscle injury. An FDA advisory panel had narrowly recommended easing access to six of seven popular peptides, and an HHS spokesperson did not immediately comment.

stories.headline: El Salvador Sends 2,000 Troops to Haiti Over Four Missing Soldiers
stories.summary:
El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti to find four nationals who went missing nearly two weeks ago, the Salvadoran foreign ministry said Wednesday. President Nayib Bukele informed Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime of the "robust deployment." The troops will also assist security efforts against Haitian gangs.

The four air force technicians, serving with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, were ambushed in an armored vehicle in the Croix-des-Bouquets area, which is controlled by armed groups. No gang has claimed responsibility. Haiti recently handed over four bodies it said were the missing men, but Bukele said they did not match: one was a child and another wore a different country's uniform.

Bukele has threatened to wipe out Haiti's gangs as he did in El Salvador if the men are not released. The Gang Suppression Force has struggled to penetrate gang-held areas, and the UN says more than 5,700 people have been killed in gang violence in Haiti this year. Tensions between the two governments have escalated over the disappearance.
